books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, Transcendentalism

primary_sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden; or, Life in the Woods (1854)

stimulus.text: Henry David Thoreau, Walden; or, Life in the Woods (1854): "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived." Thoreau built a cabin at Walden Pond near Concord, Massachusetts, and lived there for two years, from 1845 to 1847.
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim quotation from Henry David Thoreau, Walden; or, Life in the Woods (1854). Public domain; wording checked against the published text. The cabin dates are from the book's account.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Thoreau's experiment at Walden Pond most directly criticized which of the following?

options.text: A market society measuring people by earnings and possessions
The building of the Erie Canal across New York
options.misconception: Canals were the great building project of the age, so it is easy to tie any protest to them.

options.text: The growth of American literature and its writers
options.misconception: Thoreau was a writer, so it is easy to think his target was other writers.

options.text: The spread of public schools across Massachusetts
options.misconception: Schools were spreading in Massachusetts, so it is easy to make them the thing he opposed.

rationales.A: Living deliberately was Thoreau's answer to a world that priced everything, including people, by output.
rationales.B: The canal opened in 1825, twenty years before Walden; Thoreau's target was how people lived, not a ditch.
rationales.C: Thoreau wrote a book to make his point; he was not protesting books or writers.
rationales.D: Thoreau said nothing against schools; his protest was against measuring life by getting and spending.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what 'deliberately' pushes against. A life lived without thinking, chasing wages and goods.
2. Name the system behind that life. The market revolution taught people to measure themselves by output.
Background from the books: the transcendentalists protested a society that measured people by what they produced.
Remember: a protest against a way of life is a protest against the economy that shaped it.
